utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, the Trial Chamber has spent a lot of time trying to devise measures to ensure that you're able to produce the witnesses that you have. Even though come Tuesday of next week you'd have had the same time as the Prosecution, we have decided that we will continue hearing evidence up to the 9th of April. We will be taking a break, the Easter break, and we will return, I believe, on the 21st, Tuesday the 21st. So on Tuesday the 21st, we'll have the closing arguments. Now, I want to stress, Mr. Alarid and Mr. Ivetic, that when we do this, we expect the time that be used. We don't want to come and then we have a day's hearing and a witness's evidence is concluded within one session, and the rest of the day is lost. On Monday, we will be giving directions as to other time periods relating to closing briefs and so on, and I'm going to require you to give me a list day by day of how the time will be used by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: On Monday, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll let you know on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll let you know on Monday, perhaps by Tuesday. Perhaps by Tuesday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. One of the things I think might come up, Your Honour, and one of the witnesses we would like to include in that schedule; and I know it's been denied at one point, but considering Ewa Tabeau filed a clarification in the Prosecution's most recent filing, there was some additional research that was done with regards to that; and we'd still like to follow up with her on the demographic side of proof of death. So just to keep that out there, I just want to make the Court aware, and we'll probably put the request in writing, of course, but I just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't put it in writing. I will take this as an oral motion for reconsideration, and we'll give it the consideration that it requires.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a few points. Related to the -- what we're discussing now, in light of earlier orders by the Trial Chamber, we actually had made arrangements for witnesses to begin arriving here, I think next Wednesday is when the first witnesses were going to arrive, so we would appreciate guidance as soon as possible as to when we would start our rebuttal case so we don't delay any proceedings there. And, Your Honour, with respect to the rebuttal case, we were filing the motion today, but one of the witnesses we intend to call is a Dr. Chris [phoen], he is a burn expert here in the Netherlands who looked over Dr. Andersen's report and has some significant issues with it, and he also looked at the same material and is going to come and show the flaws in Dr. Andersen's report. He's only available --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Should he be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Should he be admitted as a rebuttal witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He's going to rebut with Dr. Andersen [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I'm saying if we --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, that is on the basis that we admit him as a rebuttal witness ... [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not anticipating Your Honour's rulings, but you have given us definite time, and all of these things take two, three weeks to organise the logistics. But he's only available on the 27th of March before he goes on a very extended training trip in the US and other places. So I would be asking the Chamber to consider, if it does allow us to call him, the Chamber is empowered by the rules to adjust the order of trial to, at least if the Defence have not finished calling their last witness, that this doctor be permit to be called. Your Honour, just two other brief matters. It occurred to me last evening in discussion with some staff that I think it really is inappropriate. We talked about Mr. Tabakovic and some of the other witnesses who have since they were initially Defence witnesses have made some really serious allegations against the Defence team and Mr. -- I notified the Chamber that it would be my intention to call them. Mr. Alarid said, Well, we would still like to call them. And I have no problem with who calls them, but to me it seems very inappropriate at this time given these allegations that these witnesses are then asked to sit down with the people they've made allegations against for proofing. I have no intention of proofing these people. I'm intending to introduce some video statements under 92 ter. I will let what their video statements speak for themselves. I would ask the Court to give some serious consideration to what -- possibly instructing VWS just to have them brought to the court. If Mr. Alarid wants to call them, that's fine, but I really think it would be inappropriate to require those witnesses to meet in a proofing session with the Defence at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And then one final matter, Your Honour. Yesterday, Mr. Alarid notified the Court and us that he intends -- that Mr. Lukic is going to testify. Now, I would want to ask Mr. Lukic a number of questions about Prosecution witnesses who have said -- given evidence in this case. And I don't want to -- it's an area that's ripe for confusion. There are a lot of pseudonyms, a lot of names, and I don't want a situation where I might be asking Mr. Lukic about one witness and he's thinking of another. So what I would like to do in advance of his testimony is to prepare an exhibit that just has a picture of each of the witnesses so I can say, there's VG-13, you can see VG-13, this person has said this, what do you say that that? The problem is, Your Honour, I cannot get those from the Registrar. They're not authorised to release them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, a little slower please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm asking the Chamber to authorise the Registrar to provide pictures of his own witnesses that we can create these exhibits. We would, of course, observe the protective measures and we would introduce it as a confidential exhibit when Mr. Lukic testifies. Therefore, that way everyone in the courtroom can be very clear about who we are speaking about, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, but I'll not give a ruling on that now. Later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McCoy. Before I ask my questions today, I wanted to give you an opportunity to amend any of your answers yesterday on the main points I raised with you. Perhaps upon reflection overnight, you might have reconsidered your answers. Is there anything you want to change about your statement that if there was a fire in the basement, there would be smoke plume damage on the -- above the windows on the exterior of the house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's a large, intense fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, we don't have to go through the testimony again. Is there anything you want to change or not? That's all I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is there anything you want to change about your testimony about your conclusion that the door that is presently in the house that you saw on January 25th, 2009, is the same door that was there 17 years ago?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion, yes. It is the same door.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is there anything you want to change about your conclusion that the damage that we can see on the wedge in the upper left-hand corner of the door jam has no fire damage on it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, yesterday at transcript page 5690, you said: "We came to a conclusion -- many to conclusions," I think you were saying many conclusions "... at the scene, but this document," referring to your report, "... was done in my office with peer review from my colleague, Ben Dimas." Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do I take it that you and Ben Dimas discussed the conclusions and you are in agreement with respect to the conclusions in your report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So he agrees with the conclusions about the smoke plume, the door, the wedge, the flooring?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, before I go back to talking about the flooring, I want to show you a couple of pictures that you took and ask you a couple of questions arising from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we call up Y020-3365, and I'm going to ask that two pictures be placed on the screen at the same time, but maybe if we start with this one. It's not one of the large pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, what I'm interested in here, this picture that we're looking at this is a picture of the house that is directly across from the Omeragic house, across the gully; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it was taken from the window of the basement; am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say whether it was on the insider to outside, but from that general area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P289, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if we could move this to the side of the screen, and if we could call up Y020-3401.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if we could focus on this picture, if we could maybe just zoom in a little bit on that house between the two trees, that's the same house, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we look, we can actually even see the same laundry: I don't think this person ever imagined their laundry would be shown at the Tribunal, but you can even see the same laundry hanging the clothesline; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we zoom out from this picture now again on the right. So if that's the same house, that means that the Omeragic house is either behind that tree or maybe perhaps behind the corner of that building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you zoom in again?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To the house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoom in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, relevance and beyond the scope of any expertise this witness has offered, Your Honours. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He took the pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's just asking about the photographs that he took. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm just trying to -- okay -- okay -- where would you like us to zoom in, at the house or to the right of the -- you tell us where you'd like to zoom in, and we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right below that black satellite dish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we zoom in to that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with the Omeragic house --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be to the right of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To the right if that. Just to the right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure how far, but you can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, would I be correct that if the Omeragic house was fully engulfed in flames, someone standing where you were when you took this picture would be able to see smoke from the house, no?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you can't see the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would the smoke go up into the sky, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would, but you couldn't see -- if you can't see the house, you can't say for certain if you could see the smoke plume or even flames, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. You're saying that someone standing here, if the Omeragic house was fully engulfed in fire, the roof was on fire, the basement, the ground floor, you're saying that a person here would not have any idea that there was a fire going on there? They would not be able to see smoke?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you zoom out again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And objection, Your Honour, calls for speculation and beyond the scope of direct exam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness can answer the question. If he can answer it, then let him answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I cannot see the house, I cannot say for certain if somebody in this position could see smoke or flames from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you're an experienced fireman. You drive up to a neighborhood. Have you a call for a fire. Do you need see the smoke rising from the top of the building long before you get to the house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's happened on occasion, depending on the intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's not unreasonable to think that someone could see the smoke from here; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in my expert opinion, I don't believe so. It might be possible but not very probable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. It's a dark night when the fire starts. If it was a large fire, completely engulfing the house, would somebody from here have any sensation that there's light up in the sky, light against -- light illuminating the smoke?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in the middle of the night at this particular -- from this particular balcony, I was not there at night. I don't know how much ambient light is in the air from --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not talking about ambient light. I'm talking about a house that's fully on fire. It gives off quite a bit of light, no?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And a house that's fully engulfed in fire, it's making a sound as well; is it nor? Are beams not cracking? Do we not hear the roar of the fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure there is noise associated with it. Usually the fire trucks are way noisier; on an average scene in my city the fire trucks are extremely loud compared to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it unreasonable to think that someone from this balcony would have heard --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They would not have hear it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's your testimony? Okay. Thank you. Can I tender both of the those photos, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome, Mr. Ivetic spent two hours and 30 minutes. You have now gone about two hours and 37 minutes. I'll give you another ten minutes. You must conclude within that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was an awful lot of technical problems yesterday trying to pull up these things. I don't have much more, but I will do my best to finish in ten minutes but we have a few important questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have a very proficient time-keeper, and I have no reason to doubt the accuracy of what she has -- the figures she has given me. Ten more minutes. We have move on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P290, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we call up Y020-3448.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to circle on this photograph the balcony that you took the photo from.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was either this balcony or this balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise the house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and again, I don't know if it was this balcony or this balcony at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So it's either one of the balconies you've circled. I will tender that into evidence. I'm going to ask you another question, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P291, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I call up P31. Can you turn it sideways, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, see the circle on the bottom of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's the -- it has 5, 6, or something, 6 it looks like. That's the --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That one there, yeah. That's the house you took the picture from; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Tender that into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could we call up Y020-3649.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could the Prosecution provide the reference to the exhibit number, as this is clearly a marked photograph. Is this VG-115's exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: P31 is the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: P31? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, there seems to be some problem with the technology. I'm going to ask that you look at two photographs from a book of your photographs to confirm that they're yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness be shown page 3 on the book of photographs that was introduced last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to the picture on the bottom. It's Y020-3649. Is this a picture of the Omeragic house on the left and the house next door to the right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. You want me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: 3649. It's the bottom photograph.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3649 is the top photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The bottom one.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The bottom one is 3387.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. And is that the Omeragic house on the left and the -- and the house next door on the right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe -- yes, it's the adjacent house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P292, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you to look at page 4. It's Y020-3404. Now, in picture was taken in front of Pionirska Street look up away from the town; correct.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Away from the river. There's -- the majority of the -- I mean, in the north direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, this is the roadway just in front of where the Omeragic house is; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's two or three structures between --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Between.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But this is this Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Pionirska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where you're taking this picture from is essentially the driveway to the house directly in front of the Omeragic house; correct there's a space between two houses there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P293, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can go back to talking about the floor. We finished yesterday, and you had explained what an accelerant is, and my question to you is, if someone walked into this courtroom - this a carpet, let's say there's a wooden floor underneath it - and someone were to pour five gallons of gasoline right in front of me, okay? The gasoline wouldn't soak all the way to the far side of the room, would it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the surface. If it leaned that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's say it was actually poured out right here on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So let's say it's 6, 7 litres of gasoline or a few gallons of gasoline, it wouldn't be enough to cover the entire floor?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not of a room this size, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But it would seep out in all the different directions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on how thin the layer is, it could possibly cover a room half this size, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. But it wouldn't cover all the floor. I'm trying to -- if an insufficient amount of gasoline is poured on this carpet not to cover the entire floor, some parts of this carpet will be soaked with gasoline, some will not; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if someone were to ignite that and we would allow that fire to take its natural course uninterrupted by a fire Brigade, certainly the parts soaked in gasoline would burn, and that fire would spread to the walls and to the ceiling of the room; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In a normal fire, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you as a fire investigator are called to examine this scene. If you strip out the floor, you will see a pattern of where the flammable substance was and where it wasn't; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Burn patterns, not necessarily where it was and was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, it would be a burn pattern, and that burn pattern would be more intense where the flammable liquid actually was laying on the floor and less intense or possibly non-existent on an area that was not -- did not have the flammable liquid; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but adjacent to the flammable liquid is going to burn more intense than five or ten feet away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Correct. So we could have very significant burning here, moderate burning front of you, and possibly no burning at the far left wall of this courtroom; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's look at a photograph. Y020-3618. This is one that we --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that we put a large one in front of the witness, and there's a large one for the Bench to look at as well. That could be placed on the ELMO. Could we turn it sideways.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I put some sticky notes on it to indicate the portion that I want to direct your attention to, and I don't want to mark the exhibit. I'd like to you mark the exhibit. So could we shift it over so that we could see the number 1. Could I ask you just to draw a circle just around that immediate area and remove the tag that says number 1.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the reason for the circle?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you your observations about that area.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And put 1 inside there, and you can take the 1 away. If you'd just write with your own hand 1. Now, is it your evidence that the area in circle 1 is mold and not burnt floor-board?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the inside --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Your Honour, objection, misstates the evidence as tendered. The references to mold are not references to the floor-board. In the original testimony, it was dampness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The floor was wet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's asking him his view --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It misstates the evidence. It misstates his prior evidence. He never stated with regard to those floor boards it was mold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, are you putting to the witness that he had previously said that this was mold?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My recollection was that he was saying -- and he did say rot as well. I'm concerned whether it's [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Transcript reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll [Overlapping speakers] myself to fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Reformulate the question because if you're going to refer to previous evidence, then the practice is that you must cite the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the area in the circle that you've marked number 1 -- is the pen working?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Is there fire damage in that circle?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That wood is not damaged by fire. What is it damaged by?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is damaged by -- well, for one, it is damp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's the dampness that makes it this colour?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, could we move to the area marked 2. Could I ask to you do the same exercise, draw a circle around it, put 2 in it, remove the tag.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we shift it up on the ELMO a bit so we all can see it, and the same question to you, sir, here, is in this area, is that not fire damage?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not fire damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Can we look at 3. Do the same, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That piece there. Is that your evidence that that's not fire damage?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not fire damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And 4, it's a furring -- if we could just move over and see 4. Is that against the wall, is that not a piece of furring strip affixed to the wall showing some evidence of fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, to me that doesn't look like it's affixed to the wall. It's angled --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that is not affixed to the wall. It is lying inside. Is there any fire damage on that piece?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And -- and it's not affixed to the wall. Now, let's look at A for a second.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The floor from this point back, there is not as much -- we don't have the black, the rotting, the dampness that you talk about; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence yesterday, you said that the woods would get this way because of moisture in the ambient air. Do you recall that? And that was at transcript -- 62 was the reference yesterday. I think they've renumbered it since then. But do you remember saying that was moisture in the ambient air that would cause the rot?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't remember saying exactly that, and moisture in the air does add to potential rot. This area that's black right here is under the window. Stuff away from the window is going to be less damp, okay? Just giving you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your evidence -- so is that how you would explain that some of the boards do not show these signs of this very dark appearance that you say is not fire and some do? It's the location with respect to the window.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's not my -- there was -- the majority of in room was damp. Why? I don't know. There were two windows that had been opened for 17 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is your explanation as a fire investigator as to why some of the boards seem relatively fine? They're unmarked by this dark appearance, to me what appears as charring, and some are. What's your explanation as to why adjacent boards could have such a different appearance?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were photographs of small stalagtite-looking droppings from the slab above.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So water was seeping in through the slab?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Along with close proximity to this open window.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that parts of the room are damper than others, and that's why some -- there's a difference?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could we look -- speaking of photographs, you said last night that you would look and bring us a photograph of the door jam, where the lock was inserted. Were you able to find that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said you wanted to look overnight, remember?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I did. I looked at some photos and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you find one that shows where the lock goes in?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Maybe I'll still work with this photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where's the one with the tags on it? I would tender that exhibit, and there's one that has a close-up of a board here that I'd like to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P294, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, going back to the marks that an accelerant would leave, the tell-tale sign that an accelerant was used, am I right in saying that it would be the kind of shape that you would expect if someone poured water or poured another liquid, it would kind of follow the pattern of the liquid?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you rephrase that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you talked about kind of a circular, not a -- I think -- I don't know exactly how you described the pattern --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, not corner, not solid straight lines, but more of a circular-type pour pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it would be -- it would correspond to the impression left by the -- where it was wet; correct? If someone poured the gasoline and it went out to a pattern, naturally found a pattern, it's that same pattern that would be replicated in burn marks; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at this next exhibit, and could we turn it upside down, please, or turn it the other way. Thank you. Now, I just put those yellow tags there to show you the area I want you to focus on. Could I ask you to remove them, so we can all see it very clearly. Just take them all off. That was just a temporary thing. Now, sir, here we have on the same board a combination of what I believe is charring and what appears to be wood that doesn't look like it's that compromised. Is that not consistent with the type of mark we would see if an accelerant were used?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the dark mark or the light mark?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, it's all on the same board, so it looks like part of the board has this kind of not angular shape where it's dark and some it's not. It's on the exact same board. Is this not consistent with the kind of thing you would see if an accelerant were used?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's similar but along with accelerant -- a liquid, so rain, moisture, along with darkening because of wet wood. It's liquid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can talk about other reasons afterwards. It is similar, but -- you're saying it is similar to a pattern left by an accelerant?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no obvious signs of charring.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So if the black were charring, it would be entirely consistent with an accelerant, pattern of an accelerant?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking five litres or five gallons I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's put amounts out of it. We don't know how much was used. Just you, as a fire investigator, looking at that, does it occur to you an accelerant might have been used in this case?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would be larger. It would be not just one -- this board is possibly three inches across. That's probably two inches across. It would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you as a fire investigator would look at this and say, That has no evidential significance in my investigation.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have the witness finish his answer at line 17 to 19? Mr. Groome is constantly cutting off the witness in the mid of an answer. And I think that that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was the witness himself who stopped. I don't think it was Mr. Groome who stopped him. This is at line 19, isn't it, where he says "it would be ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was the witness who himself who stopped. He stopped himself. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a few more questions, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P295, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I had given you ten minutes. You are ten minutes beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have literally six more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Six more questions? Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Unless this -- two of them, Your Honour, I just want to show two pictures, the pictures taken by this witness. If the Defence will agree to save the formality of what seems to be a very long process of trying to call them up in e-court. They're Y020-3524 and 3432. They're just two other pictures of the floor. If Mr. Alarid will agree to their admission, I would tender them and move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I would tender those two admissions. There doesn't seem to be an objection. So 3524 and 3432.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. McCoy, when there's an intense fire, let's say this was a concrete ceiling, intense fire in this room, the intensity of that fire could cause little pockets to be formed in the concrete above us, would it not, little indentations?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about spalling, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Some people like the word spalling, some don't like the word spalling; but they're essentially the intense heat causes it to expand at different rates, and we have little indentations; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The theory behind that is there's still moisture in the concrete, and when it's heated to high temperatures --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll call up the picture and get you to finish explaining that. Could we call Y020-3481. While that's being called up, please continue with your explanation of how spalling occurs.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the super-heated gases heat the moisture in the concrete, it tends to expand and crack, make little cracks like you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I'm waiting, I would also like to say that--

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: About spalling?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, relating to spalling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's up now, again it's my time. I'm limited very severely on the time.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me finish just real quick. Spalling can also take place with super cold, freezing temperatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. The top portion there, just about the centre, the centre right of the photograph, do you see the portion I'm talking about? Could you circle the --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Centre right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The centre right, the top right quadrant, there's no steel exposed. Do you see the indentations on the ceiling?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking this here?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Is that consistent with spalling?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, similar, similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. A couple more questions. I tender that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P298.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And call up 3530, Y020-3530.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And again, spalling can take place with freezing temperatures also.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. If that were the case, though, I mean, all the concrete structures in this area are subjected to the same weather conditions. It would seem to indicate we would see consistent damage on the region?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: On exterior portions of structures, yes. On interior of a home that's occupied --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's different.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because there's heat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, where is this picture taken? Is it not the area outside under the portico just to the right of the door?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, do you have other pictures similar to this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You don't recall where you took this picture?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without a reference, before and after ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask Mr. Dimas -- I'll try to find a picture and clear it up with him. Let me ask you: Is it not -- can we not see here six ends of wood coming through this concrete wall, each of them blackened as if they had been charred?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you zoom in?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Any one of those boards.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The resolution isn't that good on my screen, and again, I'm not denying the fact that there was a fire under this portico that you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Last picture I want to show you, it's reminiscent of the first picture I showed you. I'm going to ask that it be called up, 3684, and ask that a print of it be placed on the ELMO for you to examine. I have it here. Sir, the picture's up on the screen now --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's no large picture. I just have this picture I'd ask to be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is picture again of the upper floor where it was burnt out. The picture that I showed you yesterday, the tip of that timber is the one on the top right-hand corner. Are you oriented to where this picture is taken?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one yesterday is right here?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's -- yesterday, the one -- the circle you've just made. This is the remainder of the floor. We can see three other beams, two of them appear to be completely burnt out of their pocket and the on in the middle seems to have substantial fire damage but is still hanging on to the wall?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can you show us where is smoke plume damage above any of these beams on this wall?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's slightly discoloured there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you see smoke damage there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions. I tender that into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P299.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Ivetic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If we can keep this up on the screen for the moment. I'll start from backwards since this was an area I already planned on going to since yesterday Mr. Groome spent a lot of time with just the timber on the right being on the screen and zoomed in out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've identified certain signs that you believe to be evidence of the smoke plume damage on the bricks, and you had yesterday the testimony that the bricks are not as absorbent as concrete, but I'd like to pull back if we can from this picture and give Y020-3680, Mr. McCoy. And hopefully when that comes up, you'll be able to locate Mr. Groome's timber from yesterday in the middle of the picture. Now, having the full picture in front of you instead of -- and if we could zoom in on that centre portion. Zoom in some more. Not that much. Up -- one more back. There. That'd be fine. Sir, looking now at the full picture of the area of the bricks that have deteriorated above that timber from yesterday that Mr. Groome focussed on, do you see anything additional with this better view of that timber that you might consider to be the effects of smoke and/or fire evidenced on the brick?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, what I see from this picture to appear like smoke damage, and again, it's common to have V patterns, which would be a pattern like that with severe charring or heavier charring in the V that we see here, along with other -- there's more, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to the other -- to the timbers in a second. But the point, is I guess, that even decade or so of Visegrad rains has still not removed the signs of the smoke and fire damage even for this timber that Mr. Groome focussed on yesterday for the majority -- or a large portion of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I have this mark -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Ivetic. I can't understand what the witness means. In the V pattern, more charring? Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. If you have something on fire up against a wall, it will leave a V pattern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: How does it show on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. If you zoom in -- I didn't highlight the whole area, but there's damage above --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before we zoom, in I want to make sure we don't lose the markings. And I'd move to admit the markings before we zoom in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D174.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Down. I'm sorry. Up. More. More. Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have to wait and listen to the court usher, Mr. McCoy. She's -- it's best to listen to her.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is smoke damage, smoke discolouration in a V pattern above that timber. It's darker-coloured areas of the tile. Arson investigators, we're trained to read patterns. That's what leads us to the origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I fail to see it, but if you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I guess we can have this one marked, as well, since the witness has marked that up, and have that admitted as the next 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if Your Honour has follow-up questions on that, I'll defer.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D175.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- Witness, are you saying we should have seen on this photograph a V pattern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, smoke and by-products of heat and flame move up and out, okay, in a V.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] but is that visible here?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] trained eyes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My opinion, yes, and you can review this, again, with my colleague, Ben Dimas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I can't see anything, frankly. There is nothing, colour or anything different showing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is discolouration in this area. There is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: It's more damage, but it's not a colour difference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's discolouration on the bottom side of those blocks. In my opinion, that's -- that's the way a pattern is left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What you just drew, that's a V.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's a V --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that's the way the smoke went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Typically, you'll have damage in the shape of a V within the V. It's typical. Sometimes it would be an inverted V if there is an accelerant and it's a wide area on the bottom, it would be an inverted V.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] and is it your evidence, then -- that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please. Microphone. Microphone for the judge, please. Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking for you to turn it on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is it then your evidence that you would see similar Vs above the other beams?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The aspect of the underside of these blocks that are not there, that are damaged, leads me to believe that they collected and were protected, okay, from the elements, but he also collected as the smoke was going up. The smoke and heat and soot, they collected underneath and continued going up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you see it above the other beams, then, if that were to be ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. In this area, there's some there, possibly some there, some there -- and there is -- there is discolouration in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Can we have this marked and admitted as the next available 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, focussing on the timber on the right-hand side of this, you indicated there is some evidence of smoke damage. I'd like to now have photograph Y020-3681, which is a close-up taken of that exact same location. Perhaps you can see it better, and if you can describe for us what you see in the photograph when it comes up, Mr. McCoy.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is a close-up, and I see damage -- that brick is damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and again this, has been exposed to the elements, and we see yet after so many years, we still see the damage. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we have this one marked and admitted as the next 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D177.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated there's a difference between the smooth bricks and concrete. If we can have Exhibit Y020-3688, which is, I believe, a close-up of the -- of one of the other sides there on the upper levels of the house, and ask you if you could comment. Do you see anything in there of import to us after all these years on the concrete, not the red brick but the concrete above, anything that might be remnants of a fire or smoke damage.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this picture's -- I mean, this whole area --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, you're going to have to cooperate with the court officer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very probable this was damaged by smoke. This area below, I'm not sure because of the -- it's not uniform, but this area above looks more uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've touched on an important point, the uniformity of damage. Did you see anything like this down in the basement room where the fire was alleged to have been, the large fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could have this marked as the next 1D exhibit number and admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I apologise. I need to call up Y020-3639. It did receive a P number, I believe; but I can't find it in my notes, so we're going to have to go back to the original and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what you're going to see is a photograph of the -- of a portion of the wood -- of the wood door jam that Mr. Groome asked you about and asked if that was ash or if that was burn damage. And the question I have for you is, let's for the time being assume that Mr. Groome's hypothesis - and adopt it, shall we say - that this is fire damage. Would you expect the door jam to have similar damage? That is to say, would you expect there to be uniformity of the damage to this wood if, in fact, it were due to a fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fire doesn't skip. It starts and stops. Burn damage doesn't skip. It's uniform. It starts where the point of ignition is, and it continues until it stopped burning, whether it's a piece of wood or, for that matter, a forest fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so, again, in your opinion based upon the pattern of the darkening and the other damage to this wood, is this markation a result of fire damage?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now with respect to the floors, the wood floor in the basement room, Mr. Groome asked you about that, and I'd like to ask you a few things. Now, there is some talk about an accelerant being poured onto the floor and some talk about the burn patterns there. If you have a fire being started in a room where the floor has been saturated with some form of accelerant where you have 60 to 70 persons with their clothing burning for several hours, would the fire only affect the wood floor-boards where the accelerant was or wood the fire consume the wood floor-boards beyond where the accelerant was poured, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, in an area the size of the basement on Pionirska Street with that many persons and that much fuel, there would be such a thing as flashover with that much fuel, both the persons, the clothing being fuel and the accelerant being fuel, flashover is a room reaches ignition temperature; everything inside the room reaches its ignition temperature and is ignited. Every surface in this room would show charring, would show damage, fire damage, black burnt wood, every single surface with temperatures that high.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now you've used an interesting term. You've said with that much fuel, and it seems to me you're referring to the people as well. What happens when fire, intense fire begins burning a human body, human flesh, human fat. What effect does that have on a fire, especially when there's large numbers of human bodies, sir, in your experience and opinion as a fire-fighter and arson investigator?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reviewing case studies on one particular fire where over 101 people did perished in the United States, in the state of Rhode Island, the person's tissue, the person's body fat, the person's hair and clothing do becomes fuel and do ignite. They do add to the flame process, to the burning process, to the heat. They become fuel themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, with respect to one more question as to the -- actually, maybe two more questions as to the flooring.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could have --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You indicated there was moisture, and Mr. Groome asked you about the sources of moisture, and he showed you just one photograph of the ceiling. I'd like to show Y020-3621, if we can, on the e-court. And first, sir, when this comes up, I'd like to ask you if, indeed, that is a photograph from inside the basement room, the suspect room where it is alleged that this fire occurred and these people perished.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is from inside the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I could direct your attention to the exposed rebar in the ceiling, and to the left-hand side of the photograph there appears to be some white chalky substance hanging from that portion. Could you tell us -- right there. Could you tell us -- could you tell us if you observed such substances and what they were -- what they were, what that is.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That area right there, again, as I've described yesterday are stalagtites. They're tiny little, I believe, calcium crystals from the moisture dripping down from above, from the crack foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so with respect to this area of wood underneath this ceiling where the rebar is exposed and where active water is seeping in, would you expect to see more or less water damage to the wood directly below this part of the ceiling as opposed to other parts of the ceiling where there is no damage?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously more damage below this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Y020-3616, I believe it was one of the photographs that was used by Mr. Groome that we might even have a large copy of. Unfortunately, I don't have the large photographs. We don't have those capabilities, nor were we provided the Prosecution's set. But sir, on the wood there, there appears to be some kind of gloss --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We should save this one, I'm sorry. Save this one and admit it as the next available 1D exhibit number, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D179.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I stand corrected. The Y020-3616 was apparently not used by the Office of the Prosecutor. They used the other one preceding it, but I'd like to pull that up and ask the witness questions once we have a chance, and I apologise for speeding ahead. I'm trying to make efficient use of the time. This should be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the bottom right quadrant of this photograph, and if we have the large one, we can put it on the ELMO, but there appears to be some shiny glossy appearance to the wood. While you were on the scene, what was that? What was causing that effect of gloss or shininess to the wood?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, I believe it was moisture, just damp, wet wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to have this introduced into evidence if it has not already been so. Is it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D180.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, Mr. Groome asked you about this floor, and he says if -- he seemed to suggest that animals right have been walking over the floor destroying evidence of alligatoring or destroying evidence of charcoaling in the wood. The question I have for you, sir, is even if animals had walked all over the wood floor in that room, would you as an expert and would any fire arson expert be able to tell if it had been on fire or not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were extensive tests, possibly, but just visually, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So in your opinion, even if taking into account that animals right have walked over this floor, you still contend that there was not evidence of fire damage to the floor --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not what he said at all. That's not what he said at all, Mr. Ivetic. He said if there were extensive tests, possibly, but just visually, No. But you appear to be putting to him the evidence which you wish to get.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought I heard him say something more, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The evidence shows that there were areas that were not burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And lastly, there was some question of furring strips. Did you see in that basement room any evidence of any divots or holes left from furring strips in a regular pattern across the walls indicating that anything had been affixed to them at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCoy. I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. McCoy, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Dr. Linda LaGrange, Your Honour. And Your Honour, just for a little bit of housekeeping, just to inform the Court that our web mail is down, and all other access to the outside, the LiveNote we got running before court, but I tried to open web mail after the fact, and nothing's coming in on our servers so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not peculiar to you. That's affected the entire building, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. It doesn't surprise me, I guess, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit, and you may begin, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. LaGrange. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I'm fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, could you please state your full name for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: My name is Linda Shannon LaGrange.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I reside in Las Vegas, New Mexico.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I'm slowing down and my colleague is telling me to slow down because we'll have to observe pauses between my questions and answers because the translators are attempting to keep up and also the court reporter is taking down everything we say, so I'll try and go a little slower.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I'm employed by New Mexico Highlands University. I'm a full professor of experimental psychology. I'm also the associate vice-president for academic affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And please take us through your education going back to post-secondary school and tell us what it took to get where you're at today.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I attended -- well, I got my undergraduate degree in elementary education and music at the University of Alaska, and then I got a master's degree in experimental psychology at New Mexico Highlands University, and I got my Ph.D. in experimental psychology at the University of Albert in Edmonton, Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell the Court, please, what is experimental psychology and maybe differentiating what are the other fields from psychology.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, divided between clinical psychology and experimental psychology, and I think clinical psychology is what most people think of when they imagine what a psychologist does, ask that's usually psychotherapeutic interventions. Experimental psychology is broken down into several sub-fields such as neuroscience, physiological psych, psychopharmacology, psychopharmacology, so that's my emphasis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And please explain to the Court what is psychopharmacology.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Psychopharmacology is the study of the effects of psychoactive drugs on brain and behavior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what kind of psychoactive drugs are you studied particularly?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: The emphasis, at least in my own research career, was alcohol, but the instruction that I provide for students is in all psychoactive drugs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What course -- you're the vice-president in charge of academic affairs?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What are your duties as vice-President?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: My office supervises all external intramural funding for grants and research purposes, state, federal, and private. My office also supervises the graduate school, and we also supervise the institutional research office, which gathers data about the institution, and then finally we also oversee all of the off-campus centres, the campuses that aren't in Las Vegas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And also, it's my understanding that you're just simply a tenured professor?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what courses do you teach?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I still teach, actually. I try to teach one course a semester, and the courses that I try to teach every year are physiological psychology and psychopharmacology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what's a physiological psychology?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, physiological psychology is sort of the study of linking sort of the peripheral nervous system functions such as moving around, interacting with the world; with central nervous function, which is sort of the brain and processing of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I note that -- 2007 to 2008 you were in dean of graduate studies and research. What did your duties consist of as that?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, those are now subsumed under my new title, and again, the research is just processing of grant applications to funding agencies to ensure that when we send them out that they're of appropriate quality when they get reviewed at the national level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with the court usher's assistance, could we please call up 1D22-0686, a range to 1D22-0691. Now, what we have here is the CV that we tendered to the Prosecution in January of this year, but it's my understanding -- and you forwarded an updated one. What's the difference between your curriculum vitae -- oh, excuse me. It's 1D22-0668, and we got 0686 here. And that's my dyslexia written down. And what would the difference be between your -- I'm sorry, between your older CV and your newer one, while we wait?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm looking at one that I think you submitted that says June 2008, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: If that's correct, then I can update that by adding an extra review panel for NIH for the spring, and then also I believe that there are -- I'm not sure if there's -- let's see. There are three, maybe four more appearances as an expert witness listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: And I think that would be the only differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: All right. And let's try --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Alarid. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution just ask that they be provided a copy of that most current CV during the course of the break so we could review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you. And I believe the old one that we have is 1D022-0667. Let's try that one, please, and page 2 is what we would be asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to when you became an assistant professor of psychology. That's going back to 1989?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Take us through your academic experience and professor experience.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: For those first four years as an assistant professor, I was teaching full-time for the first two years, and then because I got grant funding, I had some release time, so I did a combination of instruction and research. And the courses that I taught then were psychopharmacology, which I've taught every year for 20 years; and physiological psych, which I've also taught every year for 20 years; and then drugs and behavior, research methods and statistics, and sensation of perception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, are you contesting the professor's qualifications? We have already decided to admit her as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, clearly we have no qualms with her --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have addressed myself to Mr. Weber. I'm sorry, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just as a general matter then I'll leave it to Mr. Weber to address you specifically. Some of these experts, Your Honour, we have absolutely no question. They're clearly qualified. It's the boundaries of the expertise that we do have some contention with, so I'll let Mr. Weber address the Chamber on what we believe are the appropriate boundaries of Dr. LaGrange's expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, because it's occurring to me Mr. Alarid, that we don't need to have all of this detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay, and some of it is only for the Court's benefit as opposed to qualifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And if you feel comfortable, I'm okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, with respect to the first prong that was enumerated by the Court yesterday, if the Defence is tendering her as an expert in experimental psychology, if that's the field she's being tendered in, clearly this witness is testifying currently to experience in that area. If that's the expertise that she's been tendered in, then by all means, let's admit the CV and the Prosecution has no objection to proceeding with other matters. We would still, though, contest as enumerated by Mr. Groome that the nature of this witness's expertise with respect to the second prong, she doesn't have the necessary competency to be providing the nature of those opinions that would material advance this Chamber in the system and determination of the issues are before --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And anticipating that caveat, Your Honour, one, we would have tendered her as experimental psychology but with a background in psychopharmacology as she just testified. She taught the course for 20 years, and we could go a little bit more into her focus of psychopharmacology, but it is psychopharmacology that is the reason she's here. I'm sure she'd like to perform an experiment on Mr. Vasiljevic, but that's not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I believe the witness was extraordinarily clear that a sub-set of experimental psychology is psychopharmacology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you can raise whatever you wish in cross-examination, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But it seems to us that her qualifications are undisputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, then, we'll tender her CV as the next available 1D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence, I'll simply go into a little bit more regarding what psychopharmacology is and what it can show before we endeavour into any opinions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D181.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Let's focus on psychopharmacology and specifically the effects of drugs and alcohol. Explain a little more what that's about and what kinds of different things you study and teach your students.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, I think the primary concept is that the effects of drugs and/or alcohol on the body are very specific to certain brain areas and even more specific to certain neurotransmitter systems and circuits within the brain; and so that when these students that I'm instructing graduate and are practicing in mental health fields, they are aware of the effects of both recreational drugs and therapeutic drugs and are able because of their training to make that distinction and are able to diagnose substance abuse versus just side-effects from psychotherapeutic medication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, we're going to take the break now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
