utterances.text: Yes, sir. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Half and hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Alarid, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. I'm just looking at the last bit of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. We were starting to -- just to instruct the -- or inform the Court, rather, as to what psychopharmacology is versus other fields. What's the difference between a psychopharmacologist and let's say a toxicologist or a medical doctor who's also interested in the effects of drugs and alcohol on the human being?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, there's considerable overlap, and those three examples that you gave, I guess the primary distinction at least at this point is the effects on the living person in terms of the ingestion of psychoactive drugs and their impact on behaviour. As opposed to when you talk about toxicology, you're usually implying that there was an overdose or something was tainted in the drugs, and so it's up to that expert to determine the cause of death or illness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what would a medical doctor's primary concern be with regards to alcohol ingestation or drug ingestation?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, I suspect the primary reason would be -- you know, there are a lot of sub-fields in medical doctors, as well; but if you're talking about a general practitioner, I think the primary purpose a general practitioner would have would be to identify in his or her patients abuse of a substance and then knowing where to refer that patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we have back on the screen the CV that was the last document up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just going through your primary research interests, please go through those with the Court and how those might be relevant to what you've been asked to come to court here today.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, I've done a number of different areas in research. The first one was looking at biochemical markers of excessive alcohol consumption so you could detect that a person -- in particular, what we were looking at was females who might be pregnant who were also abusing alcohol. A way to devise a simple lab test that would alert the general practitioner to the fact that this woman might be abusing alcohol while pregnant. And as you know, alcohol is metabolized very quickly, so the test had to be indirect test of some other substance that indicated a high ingestion of alcohol. And then my field also included the research into the effects of alcohol interacting with personality characteristics that might predict aggression under the -- when someone was under the influence of alcohol, and then the sort of final area that I looked at was using flavonoids to protect the foetus from alcohol abuse when in utero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Much of your work, then, is of a scientific character --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- and would require, it seems to me, a fairly strong basis in science. Looking at your CV, can you point me to the specific period when you acquired that kind of scientific basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was a graduate student at New Mexico Highlands University, my masters thesis was a biochemical thesis where I took blood samples and analysed them for different endogenous substances that might indicate the presence of personality characteristics, and then also when I was in the Ph.D. programme, I was looking at information processing and how much information a human brain can process at a single time using different sensory systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I might have been misled because your first degree was in a wholly arts field.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was in music and elementary ed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Doctor, what would be the difference between your training and the training of a neurologist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suspect that a neurologist would have more hands-on experiences with the devices that are used to image the brain and the brain functions; for instance, they'd have more experience with MRIs and CAT Scan and those kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Do you do MRIs yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Judge David.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Dr. LaGrange, if you feel related to experimental psychology in the sense of the work being done by Kerner at New Mexico School of Medicine and [indiscernible] as chairman of the psychology department during many years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Related by not identical, certainly not identical, but it's -- in the sense that it is experimental, it's close, and I'm aware of those folks. I actually was going to go to UNM to get my Ph.D. in a neuroscience program, but I chose instead to go to the University of Alberta; instead, so I met many of the folks there with the psychology and neuroscience department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: And what interrelations do you have in your field with other psychological schools. I am talking about cumulative psychology, also the psychology of meanings, you know, in other related fields. You have just talked about some interrelations and overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, well my primary relationship was not with psychology but it was with University of New Mexico's pharmacology school, and so my mentor as I was beginning my work as a professor in 1999 was Dr. Edward Dreyus [phoen] at UNM pharmacy school, and so I did almost all of my research in his lab because he had such a well-equipped biochemical lab, and so most of my collaboration has been with UNM's pharmacology school in the school of medicine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Were you a graduate student at the time that [indiscernible] was the president of Las Vegas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soon afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just focussing -- just looking at your report, I know you've taught 18 times, I'm assuming that's 18 years, as Psychology 612, psychopharmacology. Is that 18 times being 18 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's 18 years now it's 20. That's the older CV that you're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's true. That's the one I printed out. Now, with regard to psychopharmacology, tell the Court, please, about the basic pharmacological principles of absorption, distribution, inactivation, and elimination of a substance.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Part of the course, in psychopharmacology, at least what I have my students, do is to be able to determine how a particular dose, and we'll just use alcohol as an example, since that's what we're discussing, how much alcohol would be consumed to produce a certain peak on blood alcohol level. And when you're trying to find out those values, you have to take into account how the drug in this case how the alcohol was ingested. So once it's ingested, it has to be distributed throughout the body so have you to know the rate of distribution throughout the body. Once it's been distributed throughout the body, then it has to begin -- it's absorbed into the tissue. In the case, what we're interested in is brain tissue. Once that has occurred, the alcohol has to be eliminated because, in fact, it is a toxin, so in order for it to be eliminated it has to be metabolized into water soluble substances, which it is; and they have to know how that metabolization takes place, also what affects its rate, how fast it occurs, and then be able to calculate from the beginning of alcohol consumption to the ultimate elimination of all active alcohol molecules in the body. So it's ingestion, absorption, distribution, metabolization, and then elimination, and they have to know all those phases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about the cellular mechanisms involved in drug actions, and let's just use alcohol again.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, alcohol is a very interesting drug in that it has actions at particular neurotransmitter receptors, but it also interacts with cellular membranes. So it has two mechanisms of action, which are entirely different but nevertheless have profound effects on behavior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What kind of profound effects on behaviour are those?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Those are the effects that most of us can casually observe in someone who's had too much to drink, and that is loss of equilibrium in terms of motor skills and fine motor skill function as well as cognitive abilities and impulse control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what about the knowledge of a major neurotransmitter and neuroendocrine systems?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Alcohol interacts primarily with one neurotransmitter system, which is GABA inhibitory system, which is why alcohol is a depressant because it is an agonist at GABA receptors, and, therefore, if you consume enough alcohol, you have a sort of system-wide inhibition which is why it's called a depressant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And specifically, what about -- how would alcohol fall into the issue of therapeutic uses of psychoactive drugs?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, it's not used therapeutically, or at least it shouldn't be. There is some use in self-medication, but if you're psychoactive drugs to treat alcoholism; for instance, if you check into an emergency room and you've consumed too much alcohol, what they will do is put you on an IV benzodiazepine drip, because benzodiazepine act at GABA systems as well not the same receptor but on the same systems; and so you can use these therapeutic drugs to alleviate withdrawal symptoms, which in alcoholism can cause death, they are very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What other kind of withdrawal symptoms might you experience if you're an alcohol in the emergency room?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Some alcoholics will have DTs, which is a serious elevation of body temperature because of the rapid shaking, the tremors that they display. They probably won't have any memory for how they got there or what caused the situation to occur in the first place. And I don't know if you're referring to just those short-term --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How about long-term effects of DTs or detoxification?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Not so much the DTs but the long-term effects of prolonged, chronic, heavy alcohol consumption are that there's inevitably some organic damage to the brain because as I mentioned before, alcohol is a toxin; and the process of metabolizing alcohol, you also produce toxic by-products which are free radical species which will bind to lipids and membranes of the cells and cause, in some cases, irreversible cellular damage, which will result in long-term neuronal loss, particularly in the frontal cortex.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You also teach Psychology 508, drugs and behavior. Tell us about that course and why it might be relevant to what you were called here today.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: The psychopharm course is more focussed on psychotherapeutic drugs whereas drugs and behavior is a course that is offered to criminal justice majors, health majors, psychology majors; and it's sort of a general overview of, again, cellular mechanisms of psychoactive drugs, but the focus here is more on recreational drugs and drugs of abuse and signs and ways of detecting that abuse and then what to do once it's been detected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how might consumption and specially chronic consumption of alcohol effect behavior?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Are you speaking of any kind of particular behavior or just --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Generally speaking at first. We might --

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Okay. Just the long-term chronic consumption of alcohol, how might it affect behavior; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the amount we're describing as heavy, but if a person has been consuming alcohol for say 10, 15 years daily, or in -- even worse is not the daily consumption but a worse pattern of drinking in terms of negative effects on behavior is binge drinking where you achieve these amazingly high blood alcohol levels which will then have profound effects on brain function. So ultimately the person would be less able to reason, plan, problem-solve, certainly short-term memory, and to some extent long-term memory would be negatively impacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just specifically speaking, have you been published in the area of psychopharmacology and alcohol consumption and abuse?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, within just human consumption, only three times. The rest of the publications have been with indirect measures of consumption where we've assessed how much the person has consumed by self-report and then correlated that with biochemical correlates in the blood and also personality measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I note that you've been a reviewer for several publications. What are the personality and individual differences? You've been a reviewer since 1999 to the present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, I don't think we need all of this. It's in the record. Now take her to the evidence that you have brought her here to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: All right. You've been asked to provide some analysis and ultimately some opinions surrounding a Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic, and specifically what were you given to review for your analysis?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I was given the transcripts of October 23rd, 2001; October 25th, 2001; October 26th; 2001; November 12th, 2001; November 13th; 2001; and I read those transcripts and interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And that was before you prepared a summary report that was tendered to the Court?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And since --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, with regards to Mr. Vasiljevic and your review of the materials specifically related to his admissions of alcohol consumption and habits of consumption, were you -- let's focus you first on possible or probable blood alcohol levels of an individual similarly situated as Mr. Vasiljevic. And do you have some analysis to give the Court?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell the Court -- take them through your analysis step by step, and there's an ELMO there, and I know you've probably done some calculations there. If you want to put them on the ELMO at all so the Court can see, we can do that as well.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, they look like a chicken walked across -- they're just numbers and -- so I'll probably be better off just reading them and articulating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry to interrupt again, but much like the curriculum vitae, if the Prosecution could just be provided with a copy of this, we have not received that before, the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: First things first, take us through your analysis, and what do you think about the information provided by Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: (redacted) If we could just have that redacted. We're in open session. It's line 56 -- page 56, line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just for purposes of analysis, would you please give -- just using it as a range, could we used both a 750-millilitre consumption and also a 1-litre consumption?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what assumptions did you make with regards to Mr. Vasiljevic in terms of his size?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I assumed that he was 180 pounds, and then I did a standard error around that of 160 to 190, just to -- for purposes of calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So to clarify, we're using the weight and measure of pounds, and you used the range of 160 pounds to 190 pounds?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Please go ahead with your analysis.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: If his drinking pattern is as he described it, it sounds as if he were trying to achieve a certain blood alcohol level that achieved -- did what he wanted it to do. Whatever he drank, for whatever purpose, it was to elicit a certain sense; and so people who are consuming any kind of drug will consume it to a point where it meets that desired need. If he drank a litre a day throughout the day, his probable blood alcohol levels at any given time during the day would be .2 grams per decilitre, which is -- I don't know how it's reported here, but for driving it's 0.8 percent is considered the legal limit, so .2 is considerably more than the legal limit, to give a sort of frame of reference. If he drank heavily and took large doses, he could probably achieve a level of .5 grams per decilitre, which in most people would cause death, but if a person has been drinking long enough, they have built up enough tolerance that they would not succumb to such a high dose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What are the likely physiological effects on a human being at .2 grams per deciliter?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I suspect if this person had been drinking for a long period of time, if you were to observe this person at .2, because of tolerance, the motor skills and the ability to move through the world and do normal functions would not be that evident. The problem is that tolerance to alcohol is developed at different rates for different functions, so the tolerance for motor function develops quicker than the brain's tolerance for the toxicity of alcohol, so that's one of the sort of insidious dangers of alcohol consumption; heavy alcohol consumption is that you appear to be functioning fairly normally, but the brain is still in the throws of a toxic substance, and it is not developing that tolerance as quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why is there that difference?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: It's -- well, that difference exists for all drugs because different organic systems in the body respond to drugs in a different way, and of all of the systems in the body, the most vulnerable to drug insult is the brain because it has the least protection. It's just cells without any fat tissue, without any muscle tissue. It's just completely open cells, and the only thing protecting the brain is the blood-brain barrier, and alcohol gets through the blood-brain barrier with absolute ease. There's nothing about it that protects the brain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what might a -- just using that middle range of .2 grams for decilitre, what effect might that have on the brain?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: If it's done constantly, it's going to cause irreversible brain damage, particularly in the frontal lobe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, I earlier mentioned the fact that alcohol is a toxic substance as well as the metabolites creating free radicals, and so those free radicals are going to interact with cell membranes and compromise the integrity of the individual neurons in the brain. The other is that when they stop drinking, there is a rebound effect and the GABA system that had previously been stimulated by the presence of alcohol is all of a sudden under-stimulated which upsets the balance in the brain and allows excitatory amino acids, like glutamate to prevail, and when they are overactive, then the consequence is neuronal damage from excitotoxicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what kind of side effects come from this neuronal damage?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, again, the ability to plan, reason, problem-solve, and then short-term memory and long-term memory suffers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why are all these abilities and/or functions focussed in the frontal cortex?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, the frontal cortex is considered the sort of executive area of the brain, and so that the rest of the brain kind of responds to external sensory stimuli by doing what they're supposed to do; but ultimately the frontal lobe says don't run because if you run that lion will chase you. So you have this executive that keeps the rest of the brain informed, controls it, controls impulses, emotions and so it's what makes us human.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak slower when she's using medical terms, et cetera. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with regards to impulse controls and emotional issues, what impacts might some brain damage from prolonged alcohol use have on on an individual?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I should bring to your attention that the interpreter has asked you to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just in terms of executive functionings specifically relating to impulse controls and emotions, what kind of side effects might you expect with someone with this chronic alcohol use and subsequent brain damage?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Okay. The impulses are sort of generated in an area of the brain called the limbic system, and the frontal lobe, or the executive system exerts inhibitory control over the limbic system; and if the frontal lobe function is compromised or in some way reduced by degeneration, then the ability of the person to control his or her impulses is also impaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And relate -- relating back to an earlier comment you made as to teaching your students about aggression and alcohol, tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, the interest at least among my students is the cause of spousal abuse and why does alcohol consumption -- why is it so strongly associated with alcohol -- or, I'm sorry, spousal abuse, and so we're conducting research right now into what it is about alcohol consumption that causes people to become aggressive, and then specifically, we're interested in spousal abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is there any statistical data on the correlative effects between aggression and alcohol consumption?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: There is a vast amount of data on that, and what we're interested in is displaced aggression, which is less studied, and displaced aggression is -- say, for instance, a driver cuts me off and irritates me I can't retaliate against that driver, but I might go home and retaliate against a family member. If I've been drinking, it enhances that likelihood of that displaced aggression occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could other factors such as experiencing a death in one's family set off displaced aggression?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. This is not contained within the noticed opinions that are provided within this expert's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The question as posed a going into psychological experience in one's familiar. This witness was not called here today nor did she provide any opinions that relate to any type of emotional difficulties or matters that relate to her area of psychology in her report. Her report merely indicates the relationship between the effects of chronic alcoholism on Mitar Vasiljevic, so this is outside the scope of her report and the noticed opinions to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: My response to that, Your Honour, is simple, is I'm not an expert, and oftentimes when an expert's on, they say something that I think needs appropriate follow-through. I think in this particular case, there is evidence that Mr. Vasiljevic experienced a funeral the day before the Drina River of his nephew -- or his first cousin, I think it was, if I misspoke. And that combined with admissions of alcohol consumption, it seems to be relevant. That's why I followed up on it, but I hadn't thought about it until today, and I'm really posing the question to Ms. LaGrange -- Dr. LaGrange today for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We rule that the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Repeat it just to make sure that I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, there's evidence that Mr. Vasiljevic the day before -- an incident at the Drina River where he admitted that he was there and there was a killing, he had been to the funeral of his nephew who was allegedly killed in battle with enemy forces. And so along those lines, is that the kind of instigator, if you would, for displaced anger that might come into play given chronic alcohol consumption?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's precisely the example. I mean, we're using a much less profound provocation, but that's certainly within sight that kind of displaced aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you talk about displaced aggression while under the influence of alcohol or just after a long-term effects of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: All of the studies that I've read and the studies that we are doing is when they are actually under the effects of alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would you consider being under the effects of five cognacs under the effects of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I'd consider one beer sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is there any statistical data regarding increased instances of displaced aggression while under the influence of one beer to more?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: There is a positive dose response curve, so the more that is consumed, the more likely it is to have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, specifically focussing on memory impairment, tell us about the differences or potential effects on memory of long-term chronic as well as acute consumption of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, acute consumption of alcohol, if it's heavy, will certainly impair short-term memory during the time the person was under the influence of alcohol. In fact, that's what black-outs are, if a person has achieved a particularly high level of alcohol, they might continue to function fairly normally and have no memory of it the very next day, that's short-term memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What are the ranges -- is there any statistical data of when or what levels people begin to experience black-outs, although I know there could be some correlative effects on their chronic use to that?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes. It would depend on how tolerant the individual were to the alcohol itself, so if a person were alcohol-naive and then drank a bottle of wine, that person might indeed have difficulty remembering the last few drinks of that evening; whereas someone who was a chronic alcoholic would take considerably more alcohol to experience a similar kind of black-out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, can black-outs be partial as well as complete, i.e., you remember some details but not all details versus not remembering anything?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, they are on a continuum. So if someone -- say you ask a person about what happened during this time-period when he or she was under the influence of alcohol --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Like remember last night at the party.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Right. The person would say, I don't remember anything, and then if you prompted that person with particular details, then they would be able to retrieve some but certainly not all of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what about memory impairment in intoxicated non-alcoholics?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, it occurs there as well. It's just not as profound, nor is it as long-lasting because obviously there has been no real damage to the brain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, assuming someone is already under the influence of brain damage, i.e. the brain damage has become organic and it is chronic in nature, is there any effects on memory even outside the consumption of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: At a certain point, a threshold is reached where compensatory mechanisms for laying down memories and recalling them does become compromised. You know, it's not an absolute threshold. It's an individual threshold, but at some point when the damage becomes sufficient, then that person will no longer be able to retrieve all the memories that were laid down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now -- and do we have a number for that report? I'm sorry. I was on the wrong channel. I didn't realise you had your report in front of you. Now, tell us about -- let's go to the next page, please. And tell us about brain damage caused by chronic heavy consumption and would somebody who historically -- or gave a history, rather, similar to Mitar Vasiljevic experience some brain damage caused by chronic consumption?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- to the form of the question. This witness indicated that they reviewed five days of transcript. I believe the way it's phrased, that gave history, this witness is being clear that they did not ever personally interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. True. That's true, Your Honour, and I'll qualify -- I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Making the assumption that you were taking a history of a -- Mr. Vasiljevic, and he gave identical answers regarding his alcohol consumption as he did in the testimony you reviewed and the interviews that you reviewed, what would you expect?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: In terms of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Brain damage.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Okay. I would expect that -- it looks as if he were consuming this alcohol for years, and of the two drinking patterns that I mentioned earlier, that of steady, daily consumption versus binge consumption, where very, very high blood alcohol levels are achieved; the secondary pattern, the binge pattern is far more likely to result in brain damage because of the sort of initial insult of such high levels of alcohol. So what is likely to occur in the long run is that there is some brain damage to the frontal lobe and then particularly -- in particularly the circuit on the frontal lobe that connects to the hippocampus. And the hippocampus is the area of the brain that takes information that's coming in the realtime, lays it down in the form of short-term memory, and then the transfer to long-term memory occurs in an interaction with the frontal lobe. And so those are two separate processes, and both of which would become eventually impaired by long-term alcohol consumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, with the chronic alcoholic that's able to achieve very high blood alcohol levels, like you mentioned .5 grams per decilitre that would normally be fatal in a naive drinker, how -- strike that. What is the impact of the brain on extremely high alcohol levels such as that achieved between .3 and .5 grams per decilitre?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: When alcoholics consume a lot of alcohol, the alcohol we talked about earlier, ingests, distribution, absorption, and metabolization, alcohol is metabolized by enzymes in the liver, and it is done so by a mechanism called zero-order kinetics, which means that the alcohol is metabolized at a constant rate regardless of how much alcohol you ingest. Alcoholics, though, ingest way more than what that system can handle, and so there's an alternative metabolization system in the liver, called the CYP450 2E1 system that operates on first order kinetics, which means that it is concentration-dependent in terms of how much it metabolizes. The issue here is that when you kick in that 2E1 system, the by-products of that metabolic process are very, very toxic. They are the free radicals that I mentioned before that will be binding to the lipid membrane of the cells in the brain, and when they bind to those, when they -- they have an extra electron or a few electrons which makes them want to bind with molecules in the lipids in the brain. When they do that, that converts that membrane into an entirely different substance, and when it is a different substance, it can no longer function normally and allow the brain to process information normally. And if that disruption occurs time and time again, that cell dies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I pass the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I would tender the report of Dr. LaGrange that's on the screen as the next available 1D number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I have no objection to the report being marked for identification at this time subject to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D182 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you'll now cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. LaGrange.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: My name is Adam Weber from the Office of the Prosecutor. Dr. LaGrange, you were provided with materials to review in this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please make pauses between questions and answers. Please make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Already, you're being asked by the interpreter to observe the pause between question and answer. You speak particularly fast, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In forming your opinions, is it important to review all available material?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you do not have all of the materials, your opinions would be incomplete because not all the relevant information would be incorporated into your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: If I did not have them, that would be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With the material -- with the material that is provided to you, it is important to analyse all of the information that either supports or refutes a particular conclusion.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If information refutes a particular conclusion, it is important to acknowledge this information and either reconcile it or explain it.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In this case, the Prosecution was provided with a bunch of materials that were provided to you. They included many additional materials than the ones that you indicated here today. Is it correct, then, that you were not provided with the transcript of an interview with Mitar Vasiljevic from the 16th and 17th of November, 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I wish I had brought them all with me because I did bring them to the hotel room. I might not have mentioned them in the report, but I really don't remember whether I did or I did not. I know that I did not mention them in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you do not, then, rely as far as you recall on any of the statements on those two days in those interview transcripts?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're providing an opinion today that Mr. Vasiljevic's memory may have been impaired on the date of 7 June 1992 due to alcohol consumption?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: However, would it affect your opinion if you did not include the direct statement by Mr. Vasiljevic on page 55, lines 9 through 11, of the 17th of November, 2000, interview transcript in which he was asked the following question and gave the following answer: "Q. At the time of the river, you weren't drunk with alcohol, were you? "A. No, I was not drunk at that time." You did not include that statement as part of your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And you also did not include that statement as part of your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the transcript reference, it was exhibit discussed as clip 126 from 65 ter 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Had you taken account of that statement, would it have affected your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You also, then, not aware -- actually, back up. You didn't review any videos of Mr. Vasiljevic in this case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You were, then, not aware of the 19-minute-long narrative provided by Mr. Vasiljevic in which he details the events of 7 June 1992 to include in your report?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that you relied upon five days of testimony in the trial of Mitar Vasiljevic. Based on the statements in this testimony, you believe that Mr. Vasiljevic started drinking beverages in the early morning and continued throughout the day into the evening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's what he said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you state "into the evening," do you refer after -- do you mean after 5.00 in the -- p.m.?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Dr. LaGrange, you do not reference in your report that Mr. Vasiljevic stated that he no longer had a bottle of alcohol with him in the afternoon of 7 June 1992 when they spoke to Stanko Pecikoza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And because you did not review the -- or you do not recall the interview transcripts of the 16th and 17th of November, you were also not aware of Mr. Vasiljevic's statement that he went to the hotel Vilina Vlas at 4.00 in the afternoon that day after meeting Stanko Pecikoza?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Those things are not incorporated into your report?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: They are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, regardless of Dr. LaGrange's ability to recall all she reviewed, I would point to her report that is in front of you that includes the November statement, November 2001 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And for clarification, Doctor, I'm refer to November 2000 statement. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And the testimony that you provided the last couple of minutes relates to that November 2000 statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: In response to your questions that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: These statements would have been important to your calculation of Mr. Vasiljevic's blood alcohol concentration at the time of the Drina River; weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: The reports of the blood alcohol concentration were not for a specific time. They were calculated to indicate what he was trying to achieve on a daily basis to actually be able to extrapolate what those values were at a particular hour of the day would be pretty difficult; so I am saying he was achieving a steady state blood alcohol level of probably .2, and I was not making any effort to tie to it a particular event or a particular time. I'm just saying that as a matter of daily consumption, that is what he was trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just so we're clear. I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us why you did not take account of these statements to which the Prosecutor has referred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe that I had those transcripts. I think I don't have them because if it were that specific, I probably didn't. However, it wouldn't have affected what I just reported because I wasn't attempting to calculate a specific time and a specific date. I was trying to just say that this person is a chronic alcoholic would titrate his alcohol consumption in order to achieve a steady-state blood alcohol level at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have re-examination. Remember that. But can you tell us what you mean by titrating his alcohol consumption to achieve a steady blood alcohol level at all times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if you've notice had the when people smoke, now that you can't smoke inside, that they will go outside at a very predictable time, and that dose that they are taking in is called titrating. They are adjusting the dose of nicotine to a level that keeps their system comfortable. And so alcoholics do exactly the same thing. If they're really, really chronic alcoholics, they become very uncomfortable if they're blood alcohol levels goes below a certain level. They go into withdrawal. So that titration is constant dosing or dosing to maintain a constant level of alcohol in the blood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge David.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Dr. LaGrange, is there any relevance of the

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If his analysis were of his behavior in terms of aggression or violence, yes, it would have been enhanced. If it is only restricted to memory impairment, no, because that's not likely to be affected by personality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: So for instance, a chronic depression state versus a non-chronic depressive state will have the same consequences on alcohol consumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on whether the chronic state preceded the development of the alcohol problem or the alcohol problem caused the chronic because there are no non-depressed alcoholics because it causes depression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're aware based on the review of the transcripts that Mitar Vasiljevic described him as a benevolent person while under the influence of alcohol; correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mitar Vasiljevic testified for eight days of trial between 2001 and 2002?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're not aware of the three days in which he also testified in 2002?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I believe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to the materials that were provided to us, it was indicated that you were provided with the trial judgement from the case of Prosecutor versus Vasiljevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You are then not aware of testimony that was received in that case from a Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc; correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're not aware, then, that Mr. Vasiljevic was actually personally interviewed by a professional in your field?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You would agree that an expert in your field who actually personally met and interviewed Mr. Vasiljevic would be in a better position to evaluate any physical signs of chronic alcoholism that you are describing here today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I would object and ask for a clarification as to field. Was he interviewed by a psychopharmacologist or a clinical psychologist?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll be very precise about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, the doctor that interviewed Mr. Vasiljevic was a forensic psychiatrist, so slightly different field than yours. But you would agree that a forensic psychiatrist that personally interviewed Mr. Vasiljevic would be able to observe better the physical signs of the chronic alcoholism than what you did in this case?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Could you define physical signs, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, there would be physical signs of detrimental effects of chronic alcoholism; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Not necessarily unless he intervened with some kind of cognitive testing or memory testing, which I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc did perform cognitive testing on Mr. Vasiljevic. You would agree that Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc was in better position based on the administration of the cognitive testing to individually assess Mr. Vasiljevic's cognitive abilities than the materials that you were provided with in this case?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes. If he had the opportunity to test him, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If Mr. Vasiljevic successfully passed all of those test, you are not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would that affect your opinion here today?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Not unless I were allowed to administer the same tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So you would not accept the opinion of a highly qualified forensic psychiatrist in the field unless you personally saw it yourself?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You would agree in terms of the opinion you're providing today that it would have been important for you to review that prior to providing your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you even know what Mr. Vasiljevic looks like?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You agree that a Trial Chamber is capable of determining the ability of a witness to recall events --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for a legal conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please ask another question, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, here in the courtroom you would agree that the Chamber has the ability to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Same objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- see witnesses that appear before them?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat that? I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Here today we're in court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're able to see the judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, relevance, calls for legal conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. I imagine he's leading up to something. What is the concluding question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I mean, it's meritless to ask if we can see a witness. The answer is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The issue in respect to any expert that's being called is whether or not they materially assist the Chamber in the evaluation of the matters that are at hand. This witness has indicated that they never reviewed the video, didn't review a lot of other materials that were available in this case. The Chamber has an extraordinary amount of material that's in front of it in this case that relates to Mr. Vasiljevic. It would be the Prosecution's position that the Chamber is actually in a substantially better position to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not a matter for her.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, you know, but it goes to the weight that should be provide to her testimony. The fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It doesn't matter whether she agrees or not. We'll have to make up our own minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're not aware, then, that the trial judgement from the Vasiljevic case found that Mr. Vasiljevic did not suffer from diminished mental capacity?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You are also, then, not aware that there are two other eye-witnesses that were present on the Drina River on the 7th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And object as to relevance. She's not -- yeah, she's not an alibi witness, Your Honour; and she's -- beyond the scope of her opinion and direct examination as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, it is relevant as to whether or not there were people that were present that would have had the opportunity to make observations of Mr. Vasiljevic as to whether he was intoxicated or not on a particular day, a day that the accused is charged with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I mean, if she's not so aware what -- what makes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Whether or not it would have been important for her to review those materials to determine whether or not those witnesses observed any signs of intoxication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I would -- I mean, I -- the record's so big I'm not sure, but I don't believe either witness ever commented in direct questioning as to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, that's not my question [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you have been -- would you have been helped in your assessment had you been aware of two other witnesses who were present and who would have had information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that any information would have been helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Doctor, there would be noticeable signs to a trained psychologist if an individual was unable to remember an event due to alcohol consumption; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: You would think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. The individual not be able to recall the events in a logical, chronological sequence?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, unless they confabulated?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What do you mean by confabulation?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: When people have endured some kind of brain injury or assault, they try to cover it by attempting to articulate sentences that sound as if they make sense and they are logical; and some people become very good at confabulation, and you can't distinguish that they're making it up from what they're not -- isn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That is something that a trained psychiatrist could perform cognitive tests on to determine; correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Confabulation? I would suspect so. I don't know if it was included in those tests, but I'm sure you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm just asking in the abstract. That is something that can be tested for?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Then the individual would have trouble describing the temporal or spacial relationships that occurred during an event; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: They would describe them. They might not be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For example, would a person not be able to precisely recall where individuals were necessarily standing in relation to one another?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Predicated on whether or not they had brain damage? I'm kind of lost the train of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If someone's a -- there's really two circumstances that we're talking about here today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The first circumstance is whether or not the individual is a chronic alcoholic and thereby has brain damage --

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- and a diminish capacity due to that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The second scenario we're talking about today is whether or not at the time of a particular event, they have diminished capacity due to the consumption of alcohol; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So these questions relate to both scenarios, and please distinguish whether there's a difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the context of the question and based on this analysis. Mr. Weber used in cross-examination the trial finding of no finding of diminished capacity. I think from a legally question, diminished capacity has very different meanings than from a diagnosis perspective of an in-the-moment analysis; and so I think there needs to be a clarification as to diminished capacity from a legal definition versus from a diminished capacity, let's say, from a psychologist or a psychiatrist's position. They may have very different context.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a question you can ask her in re-examination. You can clarify that with her in re-examination. Judge Van Den Wyngaert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I have a question which arose from something you just said about lacunar amnesia slots that are filled up with confabulations. Is this something that you could, in a concrete case, find without seeing the person? Without having the clinical examination of the person, is this something you could conclude in the abstract, or would you have to see the person to reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could mention it as a possibility. You could not conclude anything unless you had concrete evidence right in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Dr. LaGrange, in your report, page number 2, paragraph 4, you said: "One possible explanation for this is the phenomenon known as state-dependent learning. That is a participants acquired the memories who are sober, but they were asked to recall them when intoxicated. In Mr. Vasiljevic's case, the reverse is likely to have occurred. He was intoxicated at the time of the incident. He is sober when asked to recall the details of the event." Could you elaborate even further your paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because there's a very common phenomenon that spouses or children of alcoholics have observed, and that is that some alcoholics will hide their bottles because they know that the family members will try to take them away, and if they hid the bottle of alcohol when they're sober, they can't find it when they're drunk. If they hide the bottle of alcohol when they're drunk, they can't find it when they're sober. So that kind of memory is dependent upon the state at the time that the memory was laid down, and so if they were in a state of inebriation to recall that memory, they have to also be in a state of inebriation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Would there be any circumstances by which one of these persons might deliberately try to ignore and episode, what you called confabulating while really knowing it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure that could be faked, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: So the hypothesis of confabulating does not interfere with the functioning of these mechanism? It could be other two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Dr. LaGrange, you're providing an opinion here today as to the general levels of alcohol consumption by Mr. Vasiljevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: None of your opinion today has to do with Mr. Vasiljevic's specific blood alcohol concentration on the 7th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: It did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You can not quantify his exact blood alcohol level concentration for the date 7th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just want to go back to some of the other things that an individual might have trouble explaining if they have diminished capacity due to alcohol. Would that person explain events with unexplained periods or gaps in time?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: It's certainly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would the individual have the trouble describing actions of others in detail?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's also very possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would the individual have trouble recognising individuals for whom they had never met prior to that event?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: So their only exposure to them was at that event but not any exposure before then?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You would agree that if an individual knows someone prior to an event, the effect of alcohol or the diminished capacity would have much less importance?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And especially a circumstance if one of the persons you had known for 15 years?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And the other was the person was the person that that individual stood next to as the best man in their wedding?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a couple of questions about your qualifications. You've been accepted as an expert today in experimental psychology, but as a psychologist, do you personally prescribe medications?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And psychiatrists do have different training in relation to the prescription of medications and knowing how they interrelate with the human body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct. However, in the state of New Mexico, psychologists are able to prescribe. I'm just not a clinical psychologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You are not a forensic psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: A forensic psychiatrist applies the field of psychologist to legal issues, often for the purposes of offering expert testimony on issues such as competency to stand trial and the relationship of a mental disorder to a crime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You are not a toxicologist?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: A toxicologist is an expert in the detection and calculation of poisons in the human body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to your current curriculum vitae, you have testified as an expert witness 16 times in the state courts of New Mexico; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In those 16 instances, you provided testimony in state-level prosecutions of drug or alcohol cases; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You have never provided expert testimony in a homicide case relating to the competency of an accused to stand trial?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You have never provided expert testimony in a homicide case related to the inability of an eye-witness to recall a crime based on the consumption of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How many of those cases involved an individual accused of driving under the influence of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: All but two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How many of those 16 cases involved misdemeanor charges?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't -- I don't attend to the -- whether it's a felony or misdemeanor. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, some of them may have been misdemeanor cases?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Oh, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In New Mexico, are felony cases prosecuted in the same building as misdemeanor cases?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: You'd have to ask Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, you don't know the difference?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In those cases that involve driving under the influence of alcohol, were you called as a certified breath machine operator?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Then you have never testified to the calculation of a blood alcohol concentration based on the use of one of those machines?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes, I have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You have testified to that?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I have. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have a certificate as a certified breath technician?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Is that certificate current?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: A breath technician relies on the calculation of the machine to determine the blood alcohol concentration for an individual.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this line of questioning based on relevance, outside the scope of the opinion, outside the scope of direct examination; and the witness has already testified she was not brought here to testify as to what Mr. Vasiljevic's actual breath score was at the time of the incident on the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, they are providing a calculation as to blood alcohol concentration. If she usually relies on a machine to calculate it for her as to herself, that's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree it's relevant. Let her answer the question, and then we'll take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You rely on the machine to calculate an individual's blood alcohol concentration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Usually when I'm testifying, it is to introduce the variability of the machine, and it's possible in accuracy, so I take the amount. I use a very complex equation to compute what I think the blood alcohol should be, and then I attempt to correlate that with what the machine found, so I don't use the machine. The police officer or the arresting officer uses the machine. I do the calculations myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Is that calculation either the Widmark formula or the US Department of Transportation formula that is generally accepted as a calculation for blood alcohol concentration in the United States?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes. There's Widmark, but I use Watson because it takes into account total body water which the Widmark does not, so it's considered more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Those -- the Watson test, that is not one of the two generally accepted formulas for the calculation of blood alcohol concentration in the United States, though; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: It's acceptable. It's just more complex and more accurate. It's fairly recent, 1992, and so when I do a report, I include the Widmark and the Watson and the Lewis in -- I include those three because then you get a range of possible breath scores or blood alcohol scores.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you do that in this case?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you provide that to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I did not. I did it for my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So you had that available to you prior to the 16th of January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And Judge, if I could just ask one more question before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You have never testified as an expert in psychology prior to today.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: In clinical psychology or --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Any type of psychology. You've never testified as an expert in that field prior to today.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: You'll have to define it. Because as a psychopharmacology, that's a sub-field of psychology, so I'm not sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's a very simple question, Doctor. When you've gone to court on those 16 occasions, has the Court ever accepted you as an expert in the field of psychology?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Of psychopharmacology.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So how many occasions have you been accepted as an expert in psychopharmacology?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: All but three because three were field sobriety tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say all but three, all those DUI cases you were accepted as an expert as such?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, we can take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Dr. LaGrange, I'd like to ask you some questions about your reports specifically. The first sentence of the first paragraph after your report states that it's long been known --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Dr. LaGrange, I'd like to ask you about the first paragraph, first sentence of your report. It states that: "It has long been known that high doses of alcohol having profound impact on memory." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it not a more accurate psychological statement to state that when a person is under the influence of alcohol, it cannot be said that cognitive capacity is reduced by intoxication but that a person who has taken alcohol has reduced retention, which is an element of cognitive functions?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: So you're saying that -- let me make sure I understand the question, that it's not cognition that is impaired; it's the ability to attend to that which is appropriate that is impaired?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the time of intoxication, the person maintains whatever cognitive capacity that they have at that time. It's just that they have reduced retention at that moment due to the consumption of alcohol.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: They have -- certainly. They have reduced retentional skills, or ability to allocate brain function to what is appropriate. Their cognition, although their basal ability at cognition is not impaired, their cognitive function is slower than it would be were they not under the influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that a person who is intoxicated does not have full attention capacity?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This would have an effect on quantitative capacity then of an individual to store information but have little effect, if any, on the qualitative aspects of the information that is remembered by that person. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: The qualitative memory would also be affected. In fact, we're doing a study right now on facial recognition, and that's based on qualitative evaluation of faces; so yes, quantitative probably more so than qualitative.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Doctor, I said in that question would have little effect. Is that a fair assessment of the diminished qualitative capacity of someone who is intoxicated?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I'm just thinking of studies where people who are intoxicated aren't able to evaluate appropriately other people's facial expressions. There are a number of studies out there about that, which to me is a kind of qualitative aspect in terms of right hemisphere function and recognising and threatening expression versus welcoming expression. So however you want to characterise that, that's an example -- I would characterise that as qualitative.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You reference the Yuille study in your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And that study found that there is little qualitative to an individual being under the influence of alcohol in terms of their diminished capacity.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: In terms of the paradigm of that particular study, and so when I'm responding to your questions, I'm responding in terms of other studies that had different methodology, different paradigms; and we're looking for different aspects of behavior and memory under the influence, but in that particular study, that is, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to that study, that related specifically as to whether or not eye-witnesses to a crime had diminished capacity based on alcohol; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's right. That is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And that is the only study that you reference in your report that relates to that specific topic?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your report, you reference three portions of Mr. Vasiljevic's testimony in 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The first two references in your report chronologically going through them are general statements concerning Mr. Vasiljevic's drinking; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.
