utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to your report, then, you cite a third statement. Your report states - this is in the very last sentence of the first paragraph: "When Mr. Vasiljevic was asked if he had been drinking the day of -- June 7th, 1992, he answer in the affirmative, indicating that he 'drank almost constantly.' " Is that what your report said?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You selected only three words from line 20 of that section of Mr. Vasiljevic's testimony in support of your opinion; correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Let me read to you the full section from his testimony on that date, which is the 26th of October, 2001. It's page 2131, lines 6 through 21. I quote: "Q. Mr. Vasiljevic, you were able to appreciate that the crime that occurred on the 7th of June was wrong, weren't you? "A. Yes, yes, I was. "Q. Whatever problems you remember having with your alcoholism, it did not impede your ability to know that that was wrong, what happened; is that correct? "A. No, of course. After all, they were people. No, of course it was wrong, even if you're totally drunk. Of course. "Q. Just regarding how much alcohol or when you last had alcohol at the time of the killings, when was the last time that you had a drink that day? "A. You mean before the event? Maybe an hour and a half or two. I will be sincere with you. Even when I was at work, working at the bar, I would have a sip here and there, but when I was completely off alcohol, I wouldn't drink at all. But otherwise, I drank almost constantly, and that's how I am when I drank." My question to you is, you did not include his statement that he was able to appreciate that the crime that occurred on the 7th of June was wrong in your report or here today in your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You did not include in your report or your testimony here today the fact that he indicated that whatever problems he was having with alcohol did not impede his ability to appreciate that what occurred was wrong; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: These statements are highly important to forensic diagnosis of Mr. Vasiljevic's ability to recall and appreciate the events of 7 June 1992; is that would be correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You did not include that he had stopped drinking that day about an hour and a half to two hours before the event; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That would have been crucial information to include in any analysis of his BAC on the 7th of June, 1992, because individuals eliminate alcohol from their system over time; correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, over an hour and are a half, it would be .015 percent grams per decilitre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Doctor, my question to you is whether or not that would be important.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Not really. That would be a very slight -- an hour and a half is nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, if an individual drinks alcohol over the course of eight hours, that is a much longer prolonged period than if they drank all the alcohol within three hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So that individual would eliminate alcohol from their system as they consumed more over the course of eight hours?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So someone's blood alcohol concentration would be higher, let's say, if they drank five cups of cognac within an hour period between 2.00 and 3.00 in the afternoon and then stopped drinking two hours after that than if someone drank starting at 9.00 in the morning at 5.30 in the afternoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That their blood alcohol level would be -- go back to the very first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Let's break it apart. Thank you for being patient with me. If someone drinks starting at 9.00 in the morning. They stop drinking at 4.00 in the afternoon. At 5.30, they would have a certain blood alcohol concentration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If someone started drinking five cognacs at 3.00 in the afternoon, drank all five of those cognacs by 4.00 in the afternoon, their blood alcohol concentration would be higher an hour and a half to two hours later than that person who started drinking at 9.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's probable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. Vasiljevic was not working at a bar on the 7th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, you're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your conclusion in the second paragraph, the one relating to Mr. Vasiljevic's estimated blood alcohol content, indicates that it is probable that Mr. Vasiljevic maintained a blood alcohol concentration of .1 to .2 throughout a given day. Is that an accurate reading of your report?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: It is. It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is then not probable that Mr. Vasiljevic had a blood alcohol concentration of .3 milligrams per decilitre on the 7th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Based on what you just read and what I read earlier, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So you cannot state to a reasonable degree of scientific certainty that Mr. Vasiljevic had a blood alcohol concentration of .3 on the 7th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. So with respect to your testimony here today about the effects of an individual who has .3 milligrams per decilitre of alcohol in their system, that really is not a probable conclusion in relation to Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: It's not improbable either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But it's not probable.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Not probable. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's more like likely, according to your testimony, that he would have likely been somewhere in the range of .1 to .2 based on his daily consumption?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What -- I see that based on the review of your curriculum vitae that you have experienced both administering and teaching standard field sobriety tests?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Standard field sobriety tests are generally accepted motor skills tests that are administered by law enforcement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: They measure an individual's ability to balance properly while under the influence of alcohol; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Balance and process information at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And the reason for that is that the individual who the test is being administered to is receiving directions from that law enforcement person while the test is being undertook.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: When they're performing it, there's no administration of directions. The directions are given while the person's in a particular stance, and once the directions are completed, then the person is told to implement those instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The purpose of these tests are to ascertain whether or not there are observable signs of intoxication from that individual; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: The purpose of that is to -- if they exhibit a certain number of cues is to estimate blood alcohol levels, not ability to drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You cannot scientifically precisely estimate the person's exact blood alcohol level based on the administration of these tests?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There would be certain observable signs of intoxication during the administration of these tests; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: There are if the person isn't tolerant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. And by intolerant, you're saying didn't build up a tolerance to alcohol prior to the administration of the test?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Signs that would be observable would include impaired balance?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Slurred speech?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Red, bloodshot eyes?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: They'd stumble?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to an individual that had built up tolerance, you're saying that these signs might not be observable; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would those signs at very extraordinarily high blood alcohol levels been observable, even in a person that has built up tolerance?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I've known the people at .3 to do the fields flawlessly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's not a common situation, though, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: It's very uncommon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a question in the abstract here. If two individuals described a series of events, and then separately Mr. Vasiljevic described a series of events, would it be an indication to you that Mr. Vasiljevic had a clear recollection of the events himself if his description was the same as those two other individuals, if it would be an indication to you, Doctor. I'm not asking if you can say it with certainly.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Repeat it again because I don't know if he was one of the two original individuals or they were two separate individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm saying two individuals, not Mr. Vasiljevic, describe a series of events. Independent to those two individuals, Mr. Vasiljevic also describes the same sequence of events. If Mr. Vasiljevic and these two other individuals describe the same events, would that be an indication to you that Mr. Vasiljevic has a clear recollection of the events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Describe the same events in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes. And objection, Your Honour, assumes facts not in evidence and referring specifically to the trial judgement, the transcripts of the trial. Specifically Mr. Vasiljevic was convicted because the Court found that, one, his statements were not the same as the two complaining witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's hypothetical question, and the witness is an expert. Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would that be an indication to you that Mr. Vasiljevic would have a recollection of those events?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Indeed, if he recall them independently without prompting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. And if -- all right. Thank you. I had a couple quick questions about the Yuille. Article, Doctor. It's entitled: Some effects on eye-witness memory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Page 2 of that article found that: "File-based research on the effects of alcohol on witnesses seem then and seems now to be impossible." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You only reviewed paper materials that were provide to you in a file in this case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Page 3 of that study states: "Memory for more complex events, those events with an inherent structure, are less acceptable to interference from alcohol." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That Yuille study found that: "The effects of alcohol and eye-witness recall remains speculative." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The 11 paragraphs in your report following the first two quote references to other sources; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You did not put any of these quotes from that Yuille article into your report; is that true?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. Vasiljevic has repeated the events of 7 June 1992 on at least five separate occasions?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you not aware that he immediately told his wife after the shooting at the Drina River in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you then not aware that he then reported the murders --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I would object as to the reference unless the wife testified in this trial. I'm not aware that she had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is material in evidence, Judge, from the 23rd of October, 2001, clip 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But -- yeah, but this is Mr. Vasiljevic's representations or his wife's?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If counsel would prefer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Weber. Where was that evidence given?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It was given by Mr. Vasiljevic on the 23rd of October, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That he told his wife? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you, then, also not aware that according to Mr. Vasiljevic that he then reported the murders to the police the next morning?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: If it was in the transcript, I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And was there any evidence brought in by independent references corroborating that he, in fact, reported to the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, that has nothing to do with my question right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection is that it's not a proper hypothetical for this witness consider --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, considering the fact that he's asking her to comment on self-corroboration over time, and that really doesn't go to the fact of anything, really, other than I think the Court could show that this witness could have an interest in testifying the same way over and over again considering it was his Defence. I don't -- I would respect the question much more if the wife had testified corroborating that she had told him the next day or the police had corroborated that he reported the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, I rule that the question can be answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Dr. LaGrange, are you aware that the testimony of Mitar Vasiljevic in his trial lasted over 51 hours?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Then you're not aware that Mr. Vasiljevic recounted on both direct and cross-examination during that testimony the events of 7 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You did have the transcript or part of the transcripts from that trial. You would agree that on direct examination, Mr. Vasiljevic had the opportunity to provide his own narrative of the events on 7 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On cross-examination, you would also agree that he had the opportunity to correct and reject assertions that were put to him concerning those same events?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could just briefly go under private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Dr. LaGrange, would it be an important piece of information to you as to whether or not Mr. Vasiljevic could recall the events of that day, being the 7th of June, 1992, if he was able to consistently repeat and recall those events over a number of times over the course of over eight years?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: It just indicates to me that he had a lot of rehearsal time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, you're not aware that Mr. Vasiljevic never met with the Prosecution in this case before his testimony?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's objection. Misstates the evidence. That's exactly what the interview in 2000 was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I can correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To be fair, you'd also have to put the 2002 interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I agree with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the 2000 interview, you don't recall that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to that 2000 interview, you're not aware as to whether or not the Prosecution ever met with Mr. Vasiljevic prior to that interview?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, if I could please just have one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What you're saying, then, Doctor, is that the consistent repetition and recollection of the events by Mr. Vasiljevic a number of times may simply be explained on the basis that he had the opportunity to be rehearsed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That he repeated himself several times, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not necessarily that he had a recollection quite independently of that rehearsal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That doesn't preclude that, but that doesn't actually indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to what Judge Robinson just asked you, though, wouldn't it be a simple and clear explanation that if he were able to recall the events consistently over time that he does have a memory of it?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: If that were the case, yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I mean, that would be the simple deduction based on that fact --

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- would it not? You would need additional information that he was, in fact, rehearsed or prepared in order to come to the conclusion that you're inferring to Judge Robinson here today?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware, you have none of that information that was provided to you in forming your opinion?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Dr. LaGrange, at page 58, 13 today, you indicated that irreversible brain damage would be noticeable; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: What was the context?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I don't have the exact quote in front of me, but if I put it just directly to you that would irreversible brain damage, would that be noticeable?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Not necessarily. If you had a transient ischemic attack and it just damaged a small area of the brain, you wouldn't notice it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Doctor, what I'm asking you, would that likely be noticeable?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And when I say that, are you referring to just whether or not visually to the untrained eye, would it be noticeable?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to behaviourally, cognitively, and visually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: An expert can examine someone over the course of time to determine whether or not they have irreversible brain damage?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You said that one of the long-term effects of alcohol consumption is long-term brain damage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This does not always happen; is that true?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: It does not always happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is possible for people to consume alcohol in quantities over time and not have brain damage.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Unlikely, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is possible; correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is possible for those people to remember things that happened years ago.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just because someone drinks alcohol over the course of time in quantities doesn't mean that they're going to diminish cognitive capacity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Not all of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just saying just because of that reason, that does not mean that.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Dr. LaGrange, I have brought to your attention a number of things that you did not have today in your review of the materials. Based -- in relation to the fact that you did not have all of the materials that were available, whether it be transcripts, videos, reports of other forensic psychiatrists, do you feel confident today saying beyond a reasonable degree of scientific certainty that Mr. Vasiljevic had impaired cognitive functions in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: If I base my opinion on what I read in those transcripts, I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Doctor, that's not what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Well, repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm saying now that you know that you did not have all of the materials that were available, that you did not have all the transcripts, that you did not have the videos of Mr. Vasiljevic, that you did not have expert reports and testimony on this topic, can you state to a reasonable degree of scientific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Counsel is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the context of the question as to relevance considering the fact of the narrow scope of this doctor's opinion and what she would review. Quite frankly, it's simply because of the 51 hours you add to it, all this -- a great amount of the testimony had nothing to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, the objection is without merit. Complete the question and let us get on with the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll repeat it one more time, Dr. LaGrange. Now that you are aware and you've indicated yourself that these materials would have been important to your review already in this testimony, now that you're aware of the important information that you did not have, like additional days of testimony, like transcripts of interviews, like expert reports, and relating to cognitive tests that were performed on Mr. Vasiljevic and testimony of those experts, can you say beyond a reasonable degree of scientific certainty that Mr. Vasiljevic's cognitive functions were impaired in 1992 without a review of all of those materials?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I didn't say that without the review. It was never my intention in my report to say that beyond a scientific reasonable doubt. I'm simply interpreting what I saw and saying this is what is possible, so the additional information would make me no less certain, no less doubtful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you. So it'd be wrong for either party to say, in fact, Mr. Vasiljevic's cognitive functions in 1992 were diminished based on your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Nothing further, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sure. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What is the gold standard to confirm brain damage --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What is the gold standard to confirm brain damage in an individual?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: MRI.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Outside the scope of cross. I did not bring up any testimony relating to the gold standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, how would you confirm brain damage? What is the best way to confirm brain damage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would have to do a functional MRI.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what would a functional MRI tell a diagnostician.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: When you look at it, you would be able to tell what areas of the brain were functioning at reduced capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And are there studies that have compared brain scans over a number of individuals to show the extent or lack thereof of brain damage?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, we talked about the opportunity to rehearse testimony. Can an individual include confabulation within testimony?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And even from the perception of the declarant. Could confabulation be considered and felt to be true?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: After a number of repetitions, it becomes true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And by becoming true, is that it becomes reality to the declarant?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why does that happen?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Because it happens even if you're not an alcoholic. If you repeat your perceptions of an event over and over again and you're wrong, the fact that you repeat them lays down a stronger memory than the actual event, and you begin to believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, with regards to the selected testimony, would it be fair to say that you focussed your analysis on references to alcohol consumption and the amount of alcohol consumed?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And why would the remaining 99 percent of the testimony not necessarily, be relevant to this kind of analysis?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Because this -- as I've stated before, this kind of analysis was not intended to give a precise blood alcohol level at any precise, specific time. It was looking at a person's general drinking behavior and sort of predicting based on his self-report, however accurate that was, based on that sort of describing what the blood alcohol level would be on a typical day when that person was drinking, according to his own description.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you feel as a psychopharmacologist you had sufficient information from the testimony, and most importantly, the early testimony before the Milan Lukic Defence ever got involved in things, do you feel like you have enough information from the early testimony to render your opinion?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Yes, because it's an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, I'd just like counsel to specify what particular opinion he's referencing. The doctor's given him a couple different opinions here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Let's just say opinions in plural.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, what is the difference between competency to stand trial due to diminished capacity and diminished capacity as you reference into the side effects of alcohol consumption or the secondary side effects to brain damage?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That difference would be profound. The cognitive impairment that I'm referring to is probably not something that would be immediately apparent. It just meanings that the person isn't able to recall things accurately, but doesn't mean that the person can't function as a normal human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it doesn't mean that they can't understand the circumstances of which they are under trial?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: They would not lose sight of what is right and wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so the references to the transcript where he indicates that killing people is wrong and what-not, how does that factor into things for you?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That wasn't -- that wasn't a factor at all. It had nothing to do with memory. It was a moral judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- so what other -- what kinds of things would represent diminished capacity in the context of alcohol consumption or the chronic effects of alcohol consumption?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Just the inability to recall past events with any degree of accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the Prosecution posed to you a hypothetical involving where two eye-witnesses corroborate the declarant that's the relevant declarant, and you said that that would assist you in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it change your analysis if certain relevant details were dramatically different between the two witnesses and the declarant; i.e., two witnesses say declarant had a gun and was actively involved in the shooting, and declarant says, I didn't have a gun and I stayed out of the shooting.

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to disentangle the obvious desire to claim innocence and say I didn't have the gun with an impaired ability to remember the actual situation, so it is so hypothetical I don't think I could really answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with regards to an evaluation either by a psychiatrist or a psychologist, what part of the standardised battery of testing would go to potential brain damage or loss of cognitive functioning due to chronic alcohol abuse?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I'm not sure what was administered. That's why I was asking, because there are dozens of diagnostic tools that could be used, and I'm not sure which ones were used; and I don't know if they were used to assess memory or were they used to deal with right and wrong and reasoning powers; so it's just vast, the number of tests that could be given, and I'd have to know which ones were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What tests would you give?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: If I were to do this, there are some simple memory tests, very, very simple memory tests that you can give that require testing short-term memory as well as long-term memory; and these kinds of tests are screening tests, not diagnostic tests, but they can tell you within five minutes if there is memory impairment. Then you can go further to do an MRI to verify what you suspect in your screening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with regards to a psychiatric or psychological evaluation, can the evaluation be coloured by simply what the medical professional is looking for, what is their goal during the time that they have to evaluate that person?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: I'm interpreting that question to mean that perhaps the psychiatrist was evaluating that person to determine if he was able to speak for himself adequately and was not mentally afflicted in any way that would impair his ability to understand his trial and what was going on, and if that were what was being -- what he was trying to examine or ascertain, it isn't likely that he would have focussed that much on memory. I don't know, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, what relevance is there, if any, this would be new evidence from the standpoint that upon admission on June 14th to the hospital with a broken leg that a secondary diagnosis was made of psychosis, and from a hypothetical perspective --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Weber on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection. This was not touched upon on cross-examination whatsoever, any type of secondary diagnosis, anything outside of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, what I do say to that? It doesn't arise, Mr. Weber said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid? Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You get along so well, so ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: My position is this, that the Prosecution in cross-examination did touch upon the issue by bringing up the psychiatric evaluation. To be honest, I'm not really clear on why the psychiatric evaluation was done, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let her answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For the record, we did not have an opportunity [indiscernible] certain information here. We did not have the opportunity to cross-examine her based on direct evidence, so if that could be considered by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, if the witness indicated that symptoms of psychosis were seeing things, including having a phobia to things black and seeing things black and having fear from that, this is at the time of admission, but how relevant is that to your analysis, if at all?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: What it indicates to me is he was in withdrawal when a person can, indeed, have psychotic breaks. It wouldn't have any impact on my analysis, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And how important is it for the clinician for the person during giving their history to not under or overrepresent their situation?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: The situation in terms of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, let's just say someone's going in for treatment for alcohol. Is it uncommon that they under-represent their drinking for purposes of guilt and appearance?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: That's pretty common, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I'll allow you to ask a question on that matter. Not now. When he's finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Based on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you wish, the question of symptoms of psychosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, based on her answer, I'm not going to have a question, but at the end of this I would like to make a submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is there any relevance to the synergistic effect between the chronic effects of alcohol consumption, possible brain damage, and the acute effects of being under the influence at the time?

utterances.speaker: LINDA LAGRANGE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. There's definitely an synergism. It makes the memory of short-term events even more difficult to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Doctor, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can we move to -- I want to give a decision, an oral decision. We are in public session? This morning, the Defence of Milan Lukic asked the Chamber to reconsider its decision not to allow Ewa Tabeau to give evidence. The Chamber had earlier on the 12th of March denied a Defence request to call Tabeau because it was not satisfied that she could provide any more information on the issue of alleged survivors than she had already provided during her testimony as a Prosecution witness. On the 16th of March, the Prosecution filed a notification of the outcome of further investigation regarding alleged survivors. Attached thereto is a clarification of the demographic unit prepared by Tabeau in which she explains the methodology used by her unit when verifying the death of victims and in which she gives additional information about 18 alleged survivors. The clarification contains new relevant information justifying reconsideration of the Chamber's previous decision. Tabeau may be called as a Defence witness for the purpose of giving additional testimony about alleged survivors. The Trial Chamber further notes that the Prosecution requests admission into evidence of Tabeau's clarification. The clarification is to be admitted as a public exhibit. That's the end of the decision. Mr. Alarid -- do you wish to give it a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this to be admitted as a Defence or Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's the Prosecution that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Prosecution, yes. Mr. Alarid, in relation to next week, we have to ensure that we all make the greatest effort possible to make the best use of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I can promise you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have a request for information about Wednesday because the Prosecution was bringing witnesses here for Wednesday, and they have -- they're asking whether they should bring those witnesses in light of the fact that I am allowing you to call these additional witnesses. What can you say to that? What are we to tell them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I think realistically next week is then very full if not overflowing. Just given the cross-examination of Mr. McCoy, how it flowed over in the next day, I can only assume that it will be the same with Mr. Dimas, and then if you add the issue that we have the examining psychologist for Mr. Milan Lukic as well as my police investigator who touches on a lot of separate facts that I think will deserve cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, on your word, then, I'll tell the Prosecution not to bring the witnesses, and if the witnesses -- if the time is not used ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We'll use it. I'll use it, and especially you inject Ewa Tabeau into it, we're full and we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will you reimburse the United Nations for the lost time, Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I can't afford that. This building's too big.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: From your rich resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You'd kill me. And Your Honour, practically speaking, we're not even funded for this month until someone makes a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Your friend Mr. Weber may be able to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, I didn't know if you had another matter that you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You wanted to raise another matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to make a submission to the Court, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 13th of March, 2009, the Prosecution filed a Prosecution submission regarding admission of medical records, a motion for admission of previous testimony pursuant to Rule 92 bis with annexes. Contained in this material was the Prosecution's request for the admission of the previous testimony of Dr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters. This is not possible for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- previous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You've been asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. We're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We didn't get the doctor's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc. We would just like to make a brief submission in light of today's testimony to be considered by the Chamber. We understand that the Defence still has time and an opportunity to respond to this in writing, if I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the testimony that was brought forth today, the Prosecution -- it's probative value was very minimal based on the amount of information that was provided to Dr. LaGrange. Dr. LaGrange testified very candidly before the Chamber concerning the materials that were not provided to her and the importance of other information and things that were done. Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc personally interviewed Mr. Vasiljevic over the course of two days prior to his trial in 2001. She performed a series of cognitive tests on Mr. Vasiljevic. She reached conclusions on re-examination by counsel. He brought up the issue of a psychosis. Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc fully discusses and analyses the mental condition and cognitive abilities of Mr. Vasiljevic in 1992 during the course of both her report and her testimony. The Prosecution would just ask the Chamber to further consider testimony by Dr. LaGrange today; for example, the fact that a forensic psychiatrist would be in a better position to fully evaluate Mr. Vasiljevic if they personally met with Mr. Vasiljevic and administered cognitive tests to him in their consideration of the admission of this testimony as rebuttal related to the issues that were raised today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mean you are planning to call Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc in rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We have a pending application, so I don't know -- the Prosecution [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many witnesses are you now seeking to call in rebuttal, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, that's for Mr. Groome to inform the Court of, but with respect to the pending application, the Prosecution did not raise this today to elicit a response for the Defence. We understand that Mr. Alarid and Mr. Ivetic have time to still respond to this application in writing. We would just like to provide this additional information for the Court's consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You know what the criterion is in the case law? Couldn't you have reasonably foreseen that you would need this evidence and have called it in examination-in-chief? Has it a reason ex improviso?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, on the 19th of November, 2008, we received the first witness list from Mr. Alarid. Dr. Linda LaGrange at that time was listed as a toxicology expert, not even as a psychologist. There was no factual description whatsoever of the opinions that she would be offering in this case. We had no idea that she would even offer opinions in relation to Mr. Vasiljevic. On the 26th of January, we actually got a report. That was the first notice we ever had that she would be offering any opinion in relation to Mr. Vasiljevic. So no, Judge, the Prosecution could not have anticipated that because it was something that was not known to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not going to decide now. We will consider it. The threshold as you know is very, very high, but perhaps we could just hear. What's your view on this, Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was going to change the topic slightly. I forgot to submit the report of Dr. LaGrange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you supporting Mr. Weber in his application?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: To be honest, I got to read the report. I think it's attached. I haven't read it yet. I will reserve, to be honest. I mean they can present their rebuttal normally in whatever way they can. I know it gets fuzzy when experts get involved, so please let me read the report over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I just moved for admission of Dr. LaGrange's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D182 is admitted now, and the clarification of Dr. Ewa Tabeau will become Exhibit P300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourned until Monday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd day of March, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.34 p.m.,
